title: Quantum Logic as the Logic of Contexts
authors: Haruki Emori, Atsushi Iriki, Andrei Khrennikov, Kazunori Kondo
abstract: Quantum logic is usually presented as a non-classical departure from ordinary reasoning forced on us by quantum mechanics, with classical logic kept as the secure starting point. We argue for the opposite order of explanation in a finite and fully computable setting. The free orthomodular lattice on two generators has ninety-six elements, the direct product of a six-element non-distributive factor and a sixteen-element Boolean factor. Reading the first factor as a register of contexts and the second as Boolean content, we obtain a calculus whose elements are context--bit-vector pairs and whose operations act component by component. With this calculus we establish three results. First, we classify the six layers by commutativity, identifying the central kernel of context-neutral propositions together with a dual central layer in which all complementary contexts are present. Second, we show that orthocomplementation rearranges the layers exactly as the complementation of the small factor rearranges its elements, which makes the duality among the layers rigid rather than accidental. Third, we prove that the operation forgetting the context is a surjective homomorphism of orthocomplemented lattices whose quotient is the classical Boolean algebra, so that classical logic is a six-to-one, information-losing image of the contextual calculus.
summary: This paper redefines quantum logic by treating classical logic as a derived, information-losing image of a richer contextual calculus built on an orthomodular lattice. Using a component-wise algebra over contexts and bit vectors, the authors rigorously demonstrate that contextuality is fundamental, making classical reasoning a specific, restricted limit case.
main_problem: To reverse the conventional understanding of quantum logic, arguing that classical logic is a quotient of a richer contextual quantum logic rather than being its foundation.
main_result: The paper proves that classical logic emerges as an information-losing, six-to-one image (a surjective homomorphism) from the full contextual calculus defined by the free orthomodular lattice on two generators.
method: The authors develop a context–bit-vector calculus based on decomposing the 96-element free orthomodular lattice into a direct product of a context factor and a Boolean content factor.
model_or_system: The model is an abstract algebraic structure: the free orthomodular lattice $F_2$ (with 96 elements), which is mathematically decomposed as $MO_2 	imes 2^4$. The 'contexts' are represented by the non-distributive factor $MO_2$, and the 'content' by the Boolean factor $2^4$.
key_observables: Contextuality (dependence on context/order), commutativity of sublogics, and the structure of the projection onto classical logic.
important_parameters: The size of the lattice (96 elements); the number of contexts (six layers derived from $MO_2$); the dimension of the Boolean content (four bits).
main_assumptions: Classical logic is treated as a limit or image resulting from 'forgetting' context, and structural analogies to physical processes like measurement are used.
figures_summary: The notes reference Table I showing the six-layer stratification of $F_2$ based on contexts, and Appendix A enumerating all 96 elements organized into these layers.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the algebraic model ($F_2 \sim MO_2 	imes 2^4$), defines component-wise operations in the context–bit-vector calculus, classifies the resulting six layers based on commutativity, and culminates by proving the existence of the context-forgetting projection onto classical logic.
why_interesting: While highly abstract, this work provides a rigorous algebraic framework for understanding how quantum non-classicality (contextuality) structures logical inference beyond what is captured by standard Boolean or even orthomodular logics. It offers deep structural insights into the relationship between context and truth values.
